deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: What is a contour line?
back: A line joining points of the same height. Picture water rising round a hill: each shoreline is a contour.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Hunt Map contour interval in metres mode?
back: A line every 20 m, with a thicker index line every 100 m.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Contour Vs point uphill. What is it?
back: A draw (small valley). Water runs down its middle.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Contour Vs point downhill. What is it?
back: A ridge or a spur.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Ridge: what and why it matters?
back: A long line of high ground, higher than both sides. Animals travel just below the crest; you walk below it and glass from it (Tip).

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Spur: what is it?
back: A short ridge running down off a bigger ridge, with a draw on each side. Also called a finger or point.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Draw: what does it hold?
back: Water, brush, shade and travel routes. Evening air and scent drain down it.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: How does a saddle look on a topo map?
back: An hourglass between two sets of closed rings: the low crossing of a ridge.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Why do animals cross ridges at saddles?
back: Least climbing and they stay off the high skyline (65%, hunter observation).

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Bench on a topo map?
back: Tight lines, then a wide gap, then tight lines: a flat step on a slope. Deer bed and travel there (65%).

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: How does a bench show on Hunt Map Slope steepness?
back: As an uncoloured strip (under 15 degrees) between coloured slopes.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Knob: what is it?
back: A small rounded top: a small set of closed rings. A good lookout on rolling ground.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Bowl: what is it?
back: A rounded basin with high ground on three sides; contours make big Us. A high ice carved bowl is a cirque.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Cliff on a topo map?
back: Contour lines merge or nearly touch. Small rock bands under 20 m may not show at all.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Learn each landform in which three views?
back: Topo map, Hunt Map in 3D, and on the ground.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: How do you turn on 3D on the Hunt Map?
back: Tap 3D in the pill at the bottom right. Tilt with two fingers or the tilt buttons; rotate with the rotate buttons.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Hunt Map 3D height boost range?
back: 1 to 2.5 times, default 1.5. Raise it to make benches and saddles pop.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: On an elevation profile, a flat stretch on a climb is a…?
back: Bench. A dip between two tops is a saddle.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: The fist trick?
back: Knuckles are tops, dips between them are saddles, fingers are ridges and spurs, gaps between fingers are draws.

deck: Landforms 101: ridges, spurs, draws, saddles, benches, knobs, bowls
front: Hook for the 7 shapes?
back: Really Smart Deer Sneak Between Knobs and Bowls: Ridge, Spur, Draw, Saddle, Bench, Knob, Bowl.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: Slope vs aspect?
back: Slope: how steep. Aspect: which way the slope faces (the way water would run off).

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: 45 degrees in percent?
back: 100 percent: 1 m up for 1 m along.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: 30 degrees in percent?
back: About 58 percent. 30 percent is only about 17 degrees.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: Percent slope formula?
back: tan(degrees) x 100, or rise divided by run x 100.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: Hunt Map: 3 contour lines in 100 m of ground?
back: About 60 percent, roughly 31 degrees (each line is 20 m).

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: Hunt Map Slope steepness colours?
back: Under 15 none, 15 to 25 yellow, 25 to 30 orange, 30 to 45 red (avalanche terrain in snow), over 45 purple.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: Hunt Map Slope direction: which colour is south?
back: Yellow. North is blue, east green, west red. Flat ground under 8 degrees is uncoloured.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: Noon sun height near Kamloops in mid October?
back: About 30 degrees up. On 21 December about 16 degrees.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: How much noon sun does a 30 degree north face get in mid October?
back: Almost none. A 30 degree south face gets about 87 percent strength.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: South face vs north face, in one hook?
back: South is the stove, north is the fridge.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: What grows on warm south faces near Kamloops vs cool north faces?
back: South: bunchgrass, sagebrush, open fir and pine. North: thick Douglas fir and spruce, late snow.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: BC definition of mule deer winter range slope and aspect?
back: 10 to 45 percent slope, south or west aspect, below 1,500 m in shallow to moderate snow zones (85%).

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: BC forestry warm and cool aspects?
back: Warm about 135 to 270 degrees (SE to W). Cool about 315 to 90 degrees (NW to E).

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: Cold clear morning: where to glass first?
back: Sunny east and south faces (Tip). Hot noon: shady timber.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: Why does steep broken ground matter to mule deer?
back: It is security habitat; mule deer escape up slopes into rough ground.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: Where do most avalanches start?
back: On 30 to 45 degree slopes (Avalanche Canada). They can run far out onto flat ground below.

deck: Slope and aspect: steepness and which way it faces, and why animals care
front: How did slope change hunter use in the Pennsylvania study?
back: Hunters were 1.25 times more likely to use an area for every 10 degree drop in slope.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: Elevation bands near Kamloops, low to high?
back: Bunchgrass, ponderosa pine and Douglas fir, montane spruce, subalpine fir and spruce, alpine.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: Bunchgrass zone reaches about how high?
back: Valley bottoms up to about 700 to 1,000 m.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: Interior Douglas fir zone upper edge?
back: About 900 to 1,450 m.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: ESSF (Engelmann Spruce Subalpine Fir) zone height?
back: About 1,200 to 2,300 m.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: How fast does air cool as you climb, on an average day?
back: About 6.5°C per 1,000 m.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: Clear calm night: where is it coldest?
back: The valley bottom: cold air drains down and pools (inversion).

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: What moves deer down in fall: calendar, rut or snow?
back: Snow and cold.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: BCWF (BC Wildlife Federation) mule deer study: when were most collared deer back on winter range in 2019?
back: By mid October nearly all were back.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: Deer burn the most energy in soft snow deeper than…?
back: About 25 cm of sinking depth.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: Mule deer generally avoid snow deeper than…?
back: About 50 cm.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: Moose and snow depth?
back: Move freely to about 40 cm, restricted at 40 to 70 cm.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: Where does the snowline sit higher: south or north face?
back: South face. Snow lies lower and longer on north faces.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: California quail usual height?
back: Mostly 250 to 500 m, usually below 750 m.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: Dusky grouse in fall go…?
back: Uphill to dense conifers; many observations 1,500 to 2,250 m.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: Ruffed grouse most abundant height?

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: How do you put a height on the snowline?
back: Centre the Hunt Map on the snow edge and read the elevation at the top left.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: Region 3 rule above 1,700 m?
back: Motor vehicles other than snowmobiles only on existing roads and trails. Study aid only: the official regulations are the law.

deck: Elevation bands and the snowline through the season
front: Hook for where to hunt in early snow?
back: Hunt where the white stops: just below the snow edge on warm faces.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: Spring vs seep?
back: Spring: groundwater flowing out on its own. Seep: water oozing slowly over a damp patch.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: Where do springs often appear?
back: Where a slope eases: the toe of a bench or the head of a draw, where water running along a tight layer comes out.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: Hunt Map: dashed blue line?
back: An intermittent creek: it may be dry.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: Do maps show every spring and seep?
back: No. Many are missing. Use the Satellite base, plants and your boots.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: In a dry October, what marks water on a brown hill?
back: The greenest spot: aspen clumps, willow, dogwood, brushy draws.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: Four plants that point to water?
back: Willow, red osier dogwood, cottonwood, aspen (also alder, sedge, cattail).

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: Where do trails cross a creek?
back: Where banks are low and the bottom is firm. One crossing can serve a whole slope.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: What is a wallow?
back: A muddy pit dug and rolled in by bull elk in the rut; bull moose dig rut pits too.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: Why are beaver ponds magnets?
back: Water, willow browse and cover in one place; the dam is often a crossing.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: Ranch dugout full of ducks: first step?
back: Permission, and no hunting or shooting within 100 m of an occupied dwelling or farm building.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: Dry spell vs wet spell: what do you sit?
back: Dry: water at dawn and dusk. Wet: food and cover.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: How far do deer usually live from water (studies elsewhere)?
back: Prefer within about 1 km, rarely more than about 2.4 km (65%).

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: Which way does evening air go along a creek bottom?
back: Down the creek: cold air and your scent drain downhill.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: Where do you sit at a small spring?
back: Downwind, watching the trails coming in, not right at the edge.

deck: Water on the land: creeks, springs, seeps, wallows, ponds
front: SWAMP scan list?
back: Springs, Wallows, Aspen clumps, Marsh edges, Ponds.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: What is an edge?
back: The juncture of two or more different cover types.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: What is an ecotone?
back: A soft, blended edge: forest and open land mixed through shrubs and young trees.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: What did Leopold really stress?
back: Interspersion: food and cover types mixed close together, not just more edge.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: Six edges to look for?
back: Timber and grass, cutblock, burn, field and brush, creek strip, treeline.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: Which edge shapes bunch travel?
back: Inside corners, points (fingers) of timber, islands of cover.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: BC mule deer rating: cover within how far of spring feed?
back: About 200 m.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: California quail stay within how far of cover?
back: Seldom more than 15 to 30 m.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: Mule deer security cover test?
back: Hides 90% of a deer at 60 m or less, patches 180 m or more across.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: Daily edge loop of most deer?
back: Feed in the open at dusk and night, back to cover at dawn.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: Three checks to sit an edge?
back: View of the corner, wind from the edge to you, sun at your back.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: How far off an edge do beginners sit?
back: 100 to 200 m with a rest and a backstop (Tip).

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: Hunt Map layers for edges?
back: Cutblocks by age and Burns by year, with the Satellite base.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: Downside of edges?
back: Predators and other hunters use them too; too much edge hurts some forest birds.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: EDGE hook?
back: Eat in the open, Duck into cover, Go at dusk, Exit at dawn.

deck: Edges and transitions: where two habitats meet
front: Grandpa's edge rule?
back: Do not sit in the field or in the woods. Sit where you can see both.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: A good bed gives what three things (Tip)?
back: A view below, wind from behind, cover close.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Four common bedding spots on a mountain?
back: Just below the crest on a spur or ridge, benches, heads of draws, thick cool timber.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Rough first glass for mountain mule deer beds?
back: About two thirds of the way up the face (60%).

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Mule deer security cover numbers?
back: Hides 90% of a deer at 60 m or less; patches 180 m or more across.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Which stands catch the most snow?
back: Taller than 10 m with over 60% crown completeness, like old Douglas fir.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Night thermal cover?
back: A closed canopy above 3 m: traps heat, cuts wind, catches snow.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Day thermal cover on a cold day?
back: Rock bluffs and sunny spots that gather heat.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Elk thermal cover from US studies?
back: Conifers at least 12 m tall with over 70% crown closure. Its benefit is debated (Cook 1998).

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Elk hiding cover?
back: Hides 90% of a standing elk at 61 m.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Hot day: where do deer bed?
back: Cooler north and east timber, shady benches, draw heads.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Cold clear day: where do deer bed?
back: Sunny south and east faces, below rock, out of the wind.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Windy day: where to look?
back: Lee side just below the top, in timber (Tip). Watch for swirls.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Arizona study: what mattered most for summer day beds?
back: Site temperature and canopy closure.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Douglas fir share of mule deer winter diet at Knife Creek?
back: About 62 to 89 percent.

deck: Bedding terrain and thermal cover
front: Grandpa's bedding rule?
back: Glass the beds, hunt the trails.

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: What is escape terrain?
back: The ground an animal runs to when threatened.

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: Where does a mule deer run from a coyote?
back: To and up slopes into rough broken ground, often stotting (Lingle 2002).

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: Where does a white tail run?
back: Down and away, fast, into thick cover.

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: Mountain goat escape terrain?
back: Steep slopes usually 40 degrees or more of sheer or broken cliffs.

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: How far do goats usually go from escape terrain?
back: Rarely more than 400 to 500 m, often less in winter.

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: Bighorn escape terrain?
back: Rugged rock, breaks and terraces next to steep south to southwest grass.

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: Pressured elk escape to?
back: Distance and dark timber far from roads (65%).

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: Quail escape?
back: They run to thorny brush within 15 to 30 m, then flush.

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: Before a stalk, what do you ask?
back: If it busts, where does it go? Mark the exits.

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: Animal above a cliff: shoot?
back: No. Wait until it is on ground where it will not fall (Tip).

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: Why do steep far places hold game in season?
back: Hunter density falls with slope and distance from roads.

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: Hunt Map: what shows rough escape ground?
back: Red and purple on Slope steepness (30 degrees and more).

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: What is stotting?
back: A mule deer bound with all four feet leaving the ground together.

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: Hook for deer escapes?
back: Mulie up, whitey out.

deck: Escape terrain: where animals run and why
front: EXIT hook?
back: Know the exit before entry: plan the escape route before you stalk.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Funnel vs pinch point?
back: A funnel narrows the routes; the pinch point is the narrowest spot in it.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Four families of pinch?
back: Terrain, cover, water, people.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Five terrain pinches?
back: Saddle, bench ledge, head of a draw, gap in a cliff band, narrow ridge or spur.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Bench pinch?
back: Where a wide bench narrows to a thin ledge between cliffs above and below.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Where do trails cross a steep draw?
back: Around its head, not in and out.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Cliff gap pinch?
back: The one break in a rock band: many trails, one gap.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Cover pinch example?
back: A strip of timber joining two blocks across open ground.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Best pinch spots?
back: Stacked funnels: e.g. a saddle above a timber strip above a creek crossing.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Five things to score a pinch on?
back: How narrow, between bed and feed, fresh sign, wind works for a seat, pressure.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Where to sit a pinch?
back: Off the trail, downwind or crosswind, 100 to 150 m away, clear lane, backstop.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Biggest pinch mistake?
back: Walking through the pinch, or sitting on the trail.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: No sign at a pinch?
back: No sit: map pinches are guesses until tracks prove them.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Hunt Map tool for shot distances at a seat?
back: Range rings: 100, 200, 300 m.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Upland pinch?
back: The end of a hedge or brushy strip: birds run to it and flush there.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: PINCH hook?
back: Paths join, Into cover, Narrow ground, Check the wind, Hide off the line.

deck: Pinch points and funnels deep dive
front: Grandpa's pinch rule?
back: Do not hunt where animals are. Hunt where they have to go.

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: Island of habitat?
back: A patch of good cover other hunters skip: small, close, awkward or in between.

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: Pennsylvania study: share of hunters within 0.5 km of a road?
back: 73%, on 56% of the ground: density over 2 times higher near roads.

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: Average farthest hunters got from a road in that study?
back: 0.84 km. They reported going over 2.5 times farther.

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: Four reasons good spots get skipped?
back: Too small, too close, too awkward, in between busy spots.

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: Road allowance on a road under 3 lanes?
back: 15 m each side of the middle: no shooting across or within it, no hunting within it. Study aid only.

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: The 100 m rule?
back: No hunting or shooting within 100 m of a dwelling, occupied farm or ranch building, school, church, playground or regional district park.

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: Hwy 5 single projectile band?
back: Hope to Kamloops: no single projectile within 400 m of the road allowance. North of Kamloops is not listed (my reading).

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: BC Park roads?
back: No hunting or shooting within 400 m of a park road or highway inside a BC Park.

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: Near roads, every shot needs…?
back: A solid earth backstop, never toward a road, house or trail.

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: Big game from your boat?
back: Not while the motor is propelling it (item 23).

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: Ducks from a moving boat?
back: No shooting from or with a moving boat with a motor or sail; gliding from the motor counts as moving.

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: What do some deer do when hunters walk past?
back: Slip into small cover near the road behind them (Tip).

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: Best first option for a small island?
back: Sit its edge downwind at dawn or dusk; it disturbs the least.

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: Three distances near roads?
back: 15, 100, 400: road allowance, house ring, listed highway band (metres).

deck: Islands of habitat and overlooked spots near roads
front: ISLAND hook?
back: Is it legal, Safe backstop, Look at land status, Approach with the wind, Never overhunt, Dawn or dusk.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: The 8 checks of the map read, in order?
back: Law, Access, Shape, Face, Water, Cover, Pressure, Wind.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: What comes first and last?
back: Law first, wind last.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: Law check covers what?
back: MU (Management Unit), open season, land status, parks, reserves, No Shooting Areas.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: Access check covers what?
back: Roads, gates, Motor vehicle closures, and the 1,700 m rule in Regions 3 and 8.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: Five things to notice from the truck?
back: Faces and what grows on them, burns and cutblocks, benches and saddles, green spots of water, where other trucks park.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: Why drive slowly after rain or snow?
back: The road is a tracking strip: count fresh crossings and waypoint them.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: Item 22?
back: It is unlawful to hunt wildlife from a motor vehicle.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: Item 28 in plain words?
back: No loaded firearm (chamber or attached magazine) in or on a vehicle.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: Is glassing with a rifle on you hunting?
back: Yes: searching for wildlife while in possession of a firearm counts as hunting.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: Safe way to glass from a pullout?
back: Truck fully off the road, rifle unloaded and cased, you away from the truck, or scout with no firearm.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: When can you load after seeing a deer from the road?
back: After you walk away from the truck and out of the road allowance, if all else is legal.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: Item 38?
back: No hunting with a light: no spotlight, headlamp or truck lights to hunt by.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: Before leaving home with the Hunt Map?
back: Save the area in Offline Maps on wifi; look at Satellite too.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: The scouting loop?
back: Map at home, drive and look, mark waypoints, walk and check, journal, back to the map.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: Best time to drive and scout?
back: Midday. Hunt the edges of the day.

deck: Reading land from the truck and from a map before you walk
front: Grandpa's truck rule?
back: The truck is for looking. Your boots are for hunting.
